title: The “Disappointing” Key to Impactful Teaching
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart recalls his first day as a Baltimore sixth-grade teacher, when he gave a rehearsed hooyah speech while suffering from silver bullet syndrome, the belief that one right speech, unit or strategy would make a classroom impactful. His mature conclusion is deliberately unglamorous: the key to great teaching is to faithfully show up and do the right work. Showing up fully requires an integrated, poised life in which work and family priorities align. Doing the right work requires first identifying the wrong work, meaning initiatives furthest removed from kids' long-term flourishing, without sliding into cynicism about PD. He narrows the right work to six targets: key beliefs, knowledge, argument, reading, writing, and speaking and listening. The essay is a statement of professional philosophy aimed at teachers who want to stand out.
points: Silver bullet syndrome, the hope that one perfect speech or program will transform a classroom, is the mistake most new teachers make.
Great teaching comes from the unexciting discipline of showing up and doing the right work day after day, not from standing out.
Showing up well depends on an integrated personal life in which how you work matches the priorities you profess.
Teachers cannot do everything they are asked, so the key skill is discerning wrong work, while still asking the cost of any new initiative to the work that matters.
Stuart narrows the right work to six levers: beliefs, knowledge, argument, reading, writing, and speaking and listening.
quotes: There was a part of me during those first years — and still is a part of me, sometimes — that wanted to believe that the right thing — the right speech, the right unit, the right instructional approach, the right words — was all it would take to create an impactful classroom. If I could just find “it,” then I'd finally see my students getting the kinds of results I was hoping for.

The reality, it turns out, is a little disappointing, especially for teachers who want to be special and stand out. (In other words, teachers who aren't yet aware of the work beneath the work.) The key to being a great teacher is this: faithfully show up and do the right work.

It requires cultivating an integrated, poised life, one in which the way that we're working aligns with the priorities we profess. For me, I'm most able to show up fully to work when I'm loving my wife and children the way I want to be loving them, and I'm only able to do that when I'm thinking sharply about my work and the constraints I've placed around it.

First of all, the right work can't be many of the things we're expected to do because the sum of all the things we're expected to do is more than any one person can actually do. And so the first step to doing the right work is figuring out what the wrong work is — and that's typically the kind of thing that you learn on the job.

We should never become teachers who dismiss everything we're presented with at staff meetings or professional development — cynicism isn't part of the calling. But we should always ask about the costs of new initiatives: If I start doing X, what will happen to Y and Z?

Kids tend to grow, and their flourishing tends to be advanced. And, sure, the high-stakes tests happen to go our way more than they should, too. But the tests aren't what I'm after — I'm just after faithfully showing up and doing the right work, today and then the same thing tomorrow.
